# Applications: Reception Perception (SSAC25 talk)

## Where this applies

- Inference: Grade receiver recruits by role before comparing them. Harmon says analysis must be framed by alignment and archetype, and that outside receivers on the line face more man and press while slot receivers face more zone [08:39] [09:09]. If the PFF data Baylor uses includes alignment and coverage-type splits, recruiting grades for wide receivers could weight coverage-type results by the recruit's most common alignment. Check the data fields first.
- Inference: Split football GPS demand by role before setting position thresholds. Harmon's case that two wide receivers can "might as well be playing different positions" [10:44] suggests that one wide receiver group average may hide slot and outside differences in Baylor's GPS data. This applies his role idea to GPS and is not something he said.
- Inference: Test how many games a per-game metric needs before it is stable. Harmon said he back-tested and found eight games representative of a full season [05:05] [05:35]. Baylor could run the same check on its own PFF grade or GPS per-game measures.
- Inference: When quoting percentiles in recruiting reports, state the reference group. Harmon stated that his 10th percentile is relative to players he sampled, not all college prospects [04:35].
- Inference: Consider a role-change note for receiver recruits who struggled against man coverage. Harmon said most players who went on to be high-volume receivers had a low success rate against man and press in college, then moved from outside to the slot [24:13].

## Eric's baseline

- Eric's baseline: no sport-specific or position-specific GPS or load thresholds exist in the current data dictionary, and building them is named as unfinished work. The talk extends this with a reason to split by role and alignment within a position.
- Eric's baseline: favor a small number of valid, reliable tests and keep the protocol exactly repeatable. Harmon's single-charter, fixed eight-game sample agrees with repeatability, but he shows no reliability statistics.
- Eric's baseline: a trained coach's eye matters (course team position). Harmon's film charting agrees with the idea that film-based judgment is central, and he adds a metric layer on top of it.
- The recruiting grading content otherwise has no direct link found in the method baseline.

## What would have to be true

- PFF (or Baylor's own film charting) data with alignment and coverage-type detail for college receivers.
- A set of past receiver recruits with known outcomes to see if coverage-type success at the college level relates to later role and production.
- More than a handful of players; Harmon describes 60 to 70 players per year for a national group, and Baylor's sample would be smaller.
- Someone consistent doing the charting, since assignment responsibility is unknown [22:40].

## Do not apply when

- The claim is one analyst's film charting of a sample of eight games per player, and his forecast hit rate is not shown. The Nico Collins, St. Brown and Puka examples are chosen successes; one miss (Tyler Lockett, caption "Tyro lockett's") was mentioned [20:06].
- The percentile comes from his sample, not the full college population [04:35].
- The prospect group is college players in a different scheme than Baylor's or the NFL sample used in the talk.
- A receiver's role was set by the offense (for example, a decoy route on a dagger concept [21:08]); an open or not-open tag can mislead without context.
- The information is sold as a subscription product by the speaker, which is a commercial view.

## First step

Pick five wide receiver recruits already graded at Baylor. Record each recruit's alignment split (outside, slot, on or off the line) from available film or PFF data and check whether the current grade seems fair for that role. No changes to live grades.

- Eric's baseline: favor a small number of valid, reliable tests and keep the protocol exactly repeatable. Harmon's single-charter, fixed eight-game sample agrees with repeatability, but he shows no reliability statistics.
- Eric's baseline: a trained coach's eye matters (course team position). Harmon's film charting agrees with the idea that film-based judgment is central, and he adds a metric layer on top of it.
- The recruiting grading content otherwise has no direct link found in the method baseline.

## What would have to be true

- PFF (or Baylor's own film charting) data with alignment and coverage-type detail for college receivers.
- A set of past receiver recruits with known outcomes to see if coverage-type success at the college level relates to later role and production.
- More than a handful of players; Harmon describes 60 to 70 players per year for a national group, and Baylor's sample would be smaller.
- Someone consistent doing the charting, since assignment responsibility is unknown [22:40].

## Do not apply when

- The claim is one analyst's film charting of a sample of eight games per player, and his forecast hit rate is not shown. The Nico Collins, St. Brown and Puka examples are chosen successes; one miss (Tyler Lockett, caption "Tyro lockett's") was mentioned [20:06].
- The percentile comes from his sample, not the full college population [04:35].
- The prospect group is college players in a different scheme than Baylor's or the NFL sample used in the talk.
- A receiver's role was set by the offense (for example, a decoy route on a dagger concept [21:08]); an open or not-open tag can mislead without context.
- The information is sold as a subscription product by the speaker, which is a commercial view.

## First step

Pick five wide receiver recruits already graded at Baylor. Record each recruit's alignment split (outside, slot, on or off the line) from available film or PFF data and check whether the current grade seems fair for that role. No changes to live grades.

title: "SSAC24: Evolution of Basketball Analytics: 20 Years of Nerds, Data, & Efficiency"
event: SSAC24 (MIT Sloan Sports Analytics Conference)

## Summary

A panel of four basketball analytics practitioners, moderated by Ben Alamar, traces the field from box-score work in the early 2000s to optical tracking, machine-learned play recognition and pose data. The panelists argue the biggest early shift was thinking per possession, that tracking and video let analysts speak a coach's language, and that data is often misused (small-sample lineups, correlations mistaken for causes). On player development they say numbers work best to design a player's environment, not as numbers handed to the player, and that practice data is still thin. They also argue that interviews and background checks are data that need their own reliability check. The session is history and opinion, with no datasets shown.

## Key claims

- The four factors came out of needing to estimate possessions per game, and the estimation formula had four inputs. [04:38]
- The biggest early change was getting people to think per possession instead of per game. [06:10]
- Adding up box score stats so a rebound, an assist and a point count the same was quickly seen as a poor way to value players. [10:16]
- Lineup data is misused most often: small samples and missing context such as matchups, actions and coverages. [12:25]
- Defensive rebounding was once called the most important stat because of its link to winning, but a panelist said it results from forcing misses. [12:55]
- A Celtics anecdote: the team was first in defensive field goal percentage by design while packing the paint, yet tenth in effective field goal percentage allowed, and a coach answered that the point is to score baskets. [13:25]
- Tracking data changed what analysts could tell coaches, since a box score cannot say what happened and the coaches' instructions in practice are mostly not in it. [16:55] [17:56]
- The first tracking data in a real NBA game was messy (players teleporting, misidentified), yet showed how far players ran and let the team change training right away. [18:58] [19:28]
- Second Spectrum taught a computer to recognize movements coaches care about, with a team member doing early quality checks on labels such as blitz and show. [20:32] [21:02]
- Tracking data is not perfect, and coaches challenge how plays are coded. Attaching video so the analyst can select and verify the plays was called a major breakthrough. [22:03]
- Players are receptive to data because they grew up in the age of analytics, though old habits are hard to change in the short term. [23:33] [24:34]
- In player development, one panelist says direct use of data with players is limited: the technology is not there yet and presenting data is not always the best coaching tool. [29:43] [30:13]
- The same panelist says data is better used to design the player's environment (for example plays and reads that send a player left), which is described as a bit of behavioral science. [31:15] [31:46]
- Practice data is thin, practices are few and drills are not structured enough for a computer to track. [32:16] [32:46] [37:25]
- Tracking now lets staff check many instances of a skill such as screen setting across a game instead of cutting tape for two or three. Players who sit on the bench get no game data. [36:24] [36:54]
- Roster building has a largely unexploited area: culture and what kind of teammate a player might be. [34:19] [34:50]
- Things that did not work: teams that shoot threes indiscriminately without counting what it is like to be a player who never touches the ball; and VR headsets that made users dizzy and nauseous. [26:36] [28:09]
- Predictions: pose data will bring biomechanical applications, automated officiating will arrive quickly (fouls are harder), and coaching analytics could measure how staff spend practice and film time. [41:32] [42:35] [43:05] [44:38]
- Interviews and conversations with a player's teammates and coaches are data, and a team needs a process to judge the reliability and usefulness of that data, as with three point percentage. [46:40] [48:44]
- A panelist says teams sometimes lean on basketball data over qualitative data when they should not. [47:10]
- Dean Oliver says he would have been most surprised by how fast the game changed and how differently it is played. [49:15]

## Numbers and definitions

- Basketball on Paper published in 2004 and the four factors introduced in it; the four factors are not named in the talk. [02:01] [04:38]
- NCAA season box scores back to 1983, received on paper, about 1,200 pages (caption "1,200 pages"); a later aside says "1400 pages". [05:39] [06:42]
- NBA efficiency as described: adding box score stats together. [10:16]
- Celtics: first in defensive field goal percentage, tenth in effective field goal percentage allowed (caption). [13:25]
- Tracking timeline: cameras in a few arenas including Dallas, Boston and OKC, then all 30 arenas, stated for 2010 to 2016. [14:25]
- First NBA tracking data from playoff games in 2010. [18:58]
- Hawkeye: 20 to 30 data points on a body instead of a single point. [28:40]
- Pose data: "22 body parts at 60 Herz" (caption); the next sentences on frame rate are garbled and not reliable. About five months of that data exists, of varying quality. [41:01] [41:32] [42:03]
- Coaching time split described as "8020" (caption); what the two categories are is not clear. [44:38]
- "About 50 things" can be checked about screen setting. [36:24]
- Schedule color: "three" practices in January; "five games and seven nights in five cities". [32:46] [33:16]
- One possession out of the "50" a player was in, used to show a mislabeled matchup barely changed a game score. [22:33]
- Panel banter in the introduction: a career win shares per 48 of 0.138 for one panelist and a three-point attempt rate given as "64" (caption drops the decimal). Not offered as findings. [03:06] [03:37]

## Methods and frameworks named

- Possession-based estimation and the four factors.
- Box score composites (NBA efficiency) as the approach being criticized.
- Draft models built from typed-in NCAA box scores. [06:10]
- Optical tracking from camera systems (Stats LLC cameras, Second Spectrum with its own cameras, later Hawkeye), with machine learning to label plays and human quality checks. [14:25] [21:02] [21:33]
- Play filters linked to video for verification. [22:03]
- Pose or skeletal tracking and possible eye-tracking goggles as future tools. [41:01] [44:06]
- Environment design as a way to use data with players. [31:15]
- Coaching analytics: measuring what staff spend practice and film time on. [44:38]

## Limits and open questions

- No datasets, sample sizes, accuracy figures or results were shown; nearly all claims are experiences and opinions.
- Speakers are team executives, a coach and an author, each with an institutional or commercial interest (one panelist promotes a book). [35:53]
- Auto captions do not label speakers, so some statements cannot be tied to a named panelist; here they are attributed to the panel unless the question made the speaker clear.
- One panelist says data is not used directly with players on court, while another says players are receptive; these may describe different groups. [29:43] [24:04]
- Questions on the most underutilized stats were not answered. [49:47]

## Q&A

- What did you expect to change the game but did not work out? Indiscriminate threes and VR headsets. [26:06]
- Who would have benefited from today's analytics before 2004? Shooters such as Danny Ainge (caption "Danny"), Reggie Miller and Ray Allen, and shooting big men. [37:56] [39:29]
- Which current players would thrive pre-analytics? Paint big men. [40:00]
- Will biomechanics data predict fouls? Not answered directly; automated officiating expected, fouls harder. [42:35]
- What is the most underutilized stat? Not answered. [49:47]
- When will Dean Oliver reach the Basketball Hall of Fame? Not known; Bill James of basketball comparison. [50:17]

## Summary

A panel with Paul Tudor Jones (co-founder of Sumer Sports) and Jonathan Kraft of the Patriots, moderated by Michelle Steele. Tudor Jones argues football is the hardest strategy game ever created and that a comprehensive, transparent, model-based process for player selection adds rigor and accountability, including for intangibles, which he says can be turned into numbers. Kraft agrees models help but says coaches and personnel people hold instinct that cannot be put into zeros and ones, and doubts intangibles can be digitized soon. They also discuss Sumer as customizable software that keeps each club's data private, the limits of injury forecasting, and the Patriots' move to a younger coach. Claims about the product are the speakers' own commercial view.

## Key claims

- Kraft says the Patriots' football side was built around Bill Belichick for about a quarter century, and a new direction is needed now. [03:04] [06:11]

- Kraft says the Patriots' new football operations leaders will bring more traditional analytic tools and a new grading system. [22:12] [22:43]
- Tudor Jones says everything, including leadership and smarts, can be turned into a number with rigor and process. [24:15] [24:45]
- He says a model adds three things: it is comprehensive, transparent and accurate. [25:15] [25:45] [26:47]
- He says Sumer's "Marvel" (maximize roster value) model could be a GM's, president's and owner's "best friend" by making choices explainable and cutting cost and dead cap. [28:20] [29:21] [30:23]
- He calls the current Sumer model version two and says it needs to be better by next year. [30:53] [31:24]
- Kraft says no team will match the data science staff Sumer has, so a software-as-a-service model with each club's own data in a secure environment makes sense. [32:26] [32:58]
- Kraft respectfully disagrees that intangibles can be digitized soon, citing a few thousand players a year and a couple hundred who make the league. [33:59] [34:29]
- Tudor Jones says psychographics is the hardest part of player selection because psychological tests show only small edges. [34:29] [35:01]
- He says that when two evaluators disagree on a player, each should still give a number (for example a six versus a nine) so the distinction is explicit. [36:01] [36:31]
- He says the model captures scouts' data and ranks scouts on predictive ability over time. [36:31]
- He says electronic trading in futures markets replaced human traders within a short time, and that football is on a similar path. [37:31] [38:02]
- He says the process is: the club states its offense and defense, positional weights and grades, then the model adds an injury forecast and snap counts and re-optimizes at each pick. [41:36] [42:09] [42:39]

- Tudor Jones says the model will not replace humans in football because there are too few observations. [50:30]
- Kraft recalls football people resisting a scout-accountability review years ago, and thinks they feared the technology. [51:00] [51:31]
- Tudor Jones says a planned scenario builder will let teams optimize for win now or a two to three year horizon. [52:33] [53:03]
- Tudor Jones says Brady's leadership should get a nonlinear rating because he attracted talent, and breaks football into player selection, performance enhancement, play design and in-game play. [55:39] [56:10]

## Numbers and definitions

- Stadium built for $6 million at the start of Belichick's tenure (caption "6 million"). [06:42]
- 93 of the top 100 most-watched broadcasts were NFL games; five international games in 2024 (caption). [01:31]
- Brady: sixth-round pick in 2000; Patriots had just given Bledsoe "a 100 million" (caption). [08:47]
- Sumer team size: "20 data scientists 20 engineers 15 14 person scout team" (caption, garbled). [12:57]
- Chess: 35 moves a game; football about 125 plays; 53 by 120 yard field; 10 to the 80th possible chess games. [14:34] [15:06] [15:36]
- Player selection search space: at least 10 to the 40th, up to 10 to the 170th or 180th (Tudor Jones's own estimate). [28:51] [29:21]
- Average GM lifespan of three and a half years. [28:20]
- Claimed benefits: save "millions" per team and cut dead cap space in half (no data shown). [30:23]
- Model roles: "20 big models" with submodels and variables feeding a player selection model. [26:16]
- Casino comparison: a 5% edge at least, 5 to 15% outside craps (his description). [45:49]

## Methods and frameworks named

## Limits and open questions

- No accuracy results, backtests or sample sizes are shown; the model's record is not given.

- Which metrics are undervalued at the combine? Tudor Jones passed. [54:36]

## Summary

The recurring argument is that a model is worth little unless stakeholders adopt it, so start from the right question, ship a simple version early, iterate, and deliver outputs in the format the audience already uses. The panelists also discuss model trade-offs (explainability, runtime, accuracy), generative AI with human review at ESPN, feature bias, backlog prioritization, hiring for storytelling and problem solving, and career advice. - Moore says output should be framed so it guides strategy ("10% more likely than the average to churn" versus "10% likely"). [27:04]

## Summary

Matt Harmon, creator of Reception Perception, explains his film-charting method for wide receivers, created in 2013. He charts every route and alignment from all-22 film for 60 to 70 players a year, eight games each, to isolate receivers from quarterback, line and offensive role. The main metric is success rate against coverage, read within the receiver's alignment, and he shows examples where the numbers flagged a breakout before production (Nico Collins, caption "nicoo") and where they explained role (Smith-Schuster and Brown). He concedes the game will not be fully solved, that some calls were early or wrong, and that he does not know every player's assignment. The work is his own method and subscription product.

## Key claims

- The method aims to credit receivers for routes that are not targets: a top target leader got just over 10 targets per game while running about 40 routes. [02:01]
